_problem: authorizeTenantAction (packages/db/src/authorization.ts, merged ddb69a9) is correct and tested, but the app role cannot actually call it. Measured 2026-07-31: `grep -rniw "tenants" packages/db/migrations/*.sql | grep -i "GRANT\|REVOKE"` returns EMPTY across all 27 migrations -- zero grants of any kind on the tenants table, to any role. This is not an oversight to patch with a blanket GRANT: PostgreSQL requires UPDATE privilege (not just SELECT) to run ANY row-locking clause including FOR SHARE, empirically re-confirmed 2026-07-31 on the actually-running PostgreSQL 16.14 (a SELECT-only test role fails with 'permission denied' on FOR SHARE, succeeds on plain SELECT). So `GRANT SELECT ON tenants TO app` would not be enough, and `GRANT UPDATE ON tenants TO app` would open exactly the write path authorize-tenant-action-core's own negative scope deliberately left closed: tenants.status is the tenant-root hard-override axis, and the trust-safety mechanism that must own set-and-clear together for it does not exist yet. authorization.ts's own docstring (lines 74-95, written by the prior slice's author) already names the correct fix: a narrow SECURITY DEFINER function in the style already used for every other app-restricted privileged read in this codebase (tenant_provision, auth_login_telegram, etc., 0012_auth_functions.sql) -- grant EXECUTE on a function that runs the locking read, not GRANT SELECT/UPDATE on the table itself.
_why_only_tenants_and_not_subscriptions_: Measured 2026-07-31 against information_schema.role_table_grants: app already holds SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE on subscriptions (it is in the 0009_rls_policies_grants.sql tenant_tables loop, the 'billing (tenant-scoped subset)' comment names it explicitly). subscriptions already has UPDATE, so its existing raw `SELECT ... FOR SHARE` in authorization.ts already works for the app role today and must not be touched. tenants is NOT in that loop -- it is the tenant ROOT table, not a tenant-scoped child table, so it was never a candidate for the RLS+grant-loop pattern in the first place (its rows ARE the tenants, so scoping it by app.tenant_id would be structurally wrong). Confirmed via pg_class that tenants has relrowsecurity=false and relforcerowsecurity=false -- it has no RLS at all, unlike subscriptions (both true). This means the SECURITY DEFINER function does not need to worry about bypassing RLS on tenants (there is none to bypass); it only needs to bypass the total absence of any grant.
_design_contract: Exactly one new function in exactly one new migration, following the 0012 pattern verbatim: `CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION resolve_tenant_status_locked(p_tenant_id uuid) RETURNS TABLE (status text) LANGUAGE sql SECURITY DEFINER SET search_path = public, pg_temp AS $$ SELECT status FROM tenants WHERE id = p_tenant_id FOR SHARE; $$; REVOKE ALL ON FUNCTION resolve_tenant_status_locked(uuid) FROM PUBLIC; GRANT EXECUTE ON FUNCTION resolve_tenant_status_locked(uuid) TO app;` -- LANGUAGE sql (not plpgsql) because the body is a single statement, matching auth_resolve_web_session's own shape in 0012. authorization.ts's first query changes from `SELECT status FROM tenants WHERE id = ${tenantId} FOR SHARE` to `SELECT status FROM resolve_tenant_status_locked(${tenantId})` -- a set-returning function called in the FROM position, valid Postgres syntax, no other change to authorization.ts's control flow. The FOR SHARE lock acquired inside a SECURITY DEFINER function is held for the remainder of the CALLING transaction (Postgres functions do not open their own transaction), so the existing 'lock survives past authorizeTenantAction's return' test must keep passing unmodified -- this is not this slice's decision to make differently.
_test_contract: authorization.test.ts must gain coverage proving the fix from the REAL caller identity, not just the superuser connection the existing suite uses throughout (its own top-of-file comment already names this exact gap as a known follow-up for 'whoever wires the first real (app-role) caller' -- that is this slice). At minimum: one allow-path case and one deny-path case run through `ctx.appDb.db` instead of `ctx.superuserDb.db`, proving authorizeTenantAction actually succeeds end-to-end as the app role would really call it. Additionally, a regression test proving the app role still CANNOT run a raw `UPDATE tenants SET status = ...` or a raw `SELECT ... FOR SHARE` directly against tenants (bypassing the function) -- the write path and the raw-table read path must both remain closed; only the function call path opens.
